question: Surrogacy is a medically complex process that can entail a number of risks and side effects. Before the pregnancy can begin, hormonal treatment and artificial insemination are required. Both of these procedures can also be associated with significant side effects. The psychological, ethical, legal, financial and emotional implications of surrogacy should also be emphasised.

Just recently, the UN Special Rapporteur on violence against women called for a global ban. The EU has already included the exploitation of surrogacy in its anti-trafficking directive – alongside slavery, sexual exploitation, illegal adoption and forced marriage. It referred to the need to care for victims, including through the provision of medical treatment and psychological and psychiatric assistance.

Nevertheless, according to media reports, Germany’s Commissioner of the Federal Government for Drug Policy and the country’s former Health Minister both recently used companies organising surrogacy in the US to have a child, as – unlike in the US – surrogacy is prohibited in Germany. Some media outlets have described their actions as ‘baby buying’. 1.
What is the Commission’s position on the medical, psychological, ethical, financial and legal implications of surrogacy?
Does the Commission intend to take measures to put a stop to this form of human trafficking in general?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.9.2026) The Commission is committed to upholding children and women’s rights, in full respect of its competences. Substantive family law, including rules on surrogacy, falls within the competence of the Member States.

Each Member State decides its policy and legal position as regards surrogacy, including its medical, psychological, ethical, financial and legal implications. The exploitation of surrogacy is included as a form of exploitation in the Anti-Trafficking Directive1.
The Directive targets those who coerce or deceive women into acting as surrogate mothers, without prejudice to national rules on surrogacy, including criminal and family law.
1 Directive 2011/36/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 April 2011 on preventing and

combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims, and replacing Council Framework Decision 2002/629/JHA (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2011/36/oj/eng), amended by Directive (EU) 2024/1712 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 amending Directive 2011/36/EU on preventing and combating trafficking in human beings and protecting its victims (https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/1712/oj/eng).
